lesson.title: Life's First Foothold: Primary Succession on Bare Rock
lesson.summary: Primary succession is the type of ecological succession that begins on bare substrate with no soil, such as newly exposed rock after a glacier retreats or a volcanic eruption, and it proceeds slowly because soil itself has to be built before most plants can grow.
lesson.body:
Primary succession is ecological succession that starts from essentially nothing, on bare substrate with no soil present at all. This can happen when a glacier retreats and exposes rock that has been scraped clean of any prior soil, after a volcanic eruption covers the landscape in fresh lava or ash, or after a landslide strips a slope down to bare rock. Whatever the cause, the starting point is the same: raw mineral surface, with no organic matter and none of the microorganisms and nutrients that most plants depend on to grow.

Because there is no soil to begin with, the first colonizers of a primary succession site have to be species that can survive directly on bare rock, and lichens are the organisms most often described in this role. A lichen is actually a partnership between a fungus and a photosynthetic partner, usually algae or cyanobacteria, living together in a single structure, and this partnership allows lichens to grow on bare rock surfaces where almost nothing else can establish itself, slowly extracting a small amount of nutrients from the rock and from rainfall and dust. Mosses often colonize alongside or shortly after lichens for similar reasons. As lichens and mosses grow, die, and decompose, and as small amounts of windblown dust and organic debris accumulate around them, a very thin layer of primitive soil gradually begins to form. This process of soil building from bare rock can take a genuinely long time, plausibly many decades to centuries depending on climate and conditions, since it depends on slow physical weathering of the rock as well as the gradual buildup of organic matter.

Once even a thin soil layer exists, it becomes possible for small herbaceous plants and grasses to take root, species that could never have survived on the bare rock itself. As these plants grow and die, they add more organic matter to the developing soil, deepening and enriching it further. This, in turn, allows larger plants, shrubs, and eventually trees to establish, and as vegetation becomes taller and more complex, animal species that depend on that vegetation for food and shelter move in as well. Glacier Bay in Alaska, where retreating glaciers have exposed a long sequence of progressively older bare ground over roughly the last two centuries, is one of the most studied real world sites for observing this kind of long term primary succession, since researchers can compare areas of different ages, from very recently exposed rock near the current glacier front to older ground further away that has had more time to develop soil and vegetation.

Primary succession connects directly back to the general pattern described in the previous chapter: an unstable, low diversity starting community, in this case just a handful of tough colonizing species like lichens, is gradually replaced by an increasingly diverse and structurally complex community as conditions improve. What makes primary succession distinctive, and typically far slower than the secondary succession covered next, is that so much of that early time is spent simply building soil from nothing, a foundational step that secondary succession, starting from ground that already has soil, does not need to repeat.
